title: Finding Evidence - Guided Practice
description: Learn to match evidence to the exact claim it supports, separate direct evidence from merely related details, and verify the connection across an argument.
subject: rla
passage:
Riverton Distribution Center tested staggered start times for eight weeks after supervisors reported long truck queues and crowded employee entrances at 7:00 a.m. Under the pilot, half of the morning warehouse crew began at 6:30, while the rest began at 7:15. Operations manager Elena Park recommends continuing the staggered schedule for six more months while the center collects data across busier and slower seasons. She argues that the pilot reduced loading-area congestion, improved employee punctuality, and did so without meaningfully reducing productivity or changing the center's basic staffing level.

The clearest evidence concerns congestion. Before the pilot, 38 percent of inbound trucks arriving between 6:45 and 7:30 waited more than fifteen minutes before reaching an open bay. During the eight-week pilot, that share fell to 17 percent. Supervisors also counted an average of twenty-six vehicles in the entrance queue at 7:05 before the change, compared with fourteen during the pilot. Park says those measures matter because the schedule was designed to spread the morning arrival rush rather than increase the number of loading bays.

Park also points to employee punctuality. During the eight weeks before the pilot, 11.8 percent of morning clock-ins were more than five minutes late. During the staggered schedule, the rate was 6.4 percent. A follow-up survey found that some employees on the 7:15 start said they could use a later public-bus connection instead of paying for a ride when they missed the earlier bus. However, Park does not use the survey alone as proof of improved punctuality; the clock-in records are the direct measure of whether workers arrived on time.

Productivity data are less dramatic but still important to Park's recommendation. The center processed 21.4 orders per labor hour during the eight weeks before the pilot and 21.1 during the pilot. The number of damaged-order reports also remained nearly unchanged. Park interprets those results cautiously: the staggered schedule did not increase output, but the center appears to have reduced congestion and lateness without a large productivity loss. She therefore rejects the claim that the pilot succeeded because it made employees work faster.

The pilot has limits. It took place during a relatively steady shipping period, not the holiday peak, and employees could request which start time they preferred. A construction project on a nearby road also ended during the third week, which may have reduced some traffic outside the facility. Park says these factors are reasons to keep measuring rather than reasons to discard the pilot. A six-month extension would let the center compare results across heavier demand and less favorable travel conditions. If truck waiting and late clock-ins remain lower while productivity stays close to its previous level, Park argues, the evidence would be strong enough to consider making staggered starts permanent.

questions.prompt: Match each passage detail to the claim it most directly supports.
questions.explanation: The truck-wait and queue measures function as evidence for congestion, while clock-in records function as evidence for punctuality. Park’s recommendation is a claim about what the center should do next, not evidence for either benefit.
questions.rule: Evidence can be strong and still belong to the wrong claim. Name the claim first, then ask what the detail actually measures.
questions.hint: For each result, identify exactly what was counted or recorded—waiting trucks, employee clock-ins, or another measure. Match that measurement to the claim it can actually test, not merely a sentence on the same topic.

items.text: The share of inbound trucks waiting more than fifteen minutes fell from 38 percent to 17 percent.
Late morning clock-ins fell from 11.8 percent to 6.4 percent.
Park recommends continuing the staggered schedule for six more months.
The average 7:05 entrance queue fell from twenty-six vehicles to fourteen.

questions.prompt: Which sentence gives the most direct evidence for Park's claim that punctuality improved during the staggered schedule?
questions.explanation: This result is the direct outcome measure for the claim about improved punctuality. The survey offers a possible explanation, but the clock-in rate is what records whether late arrivals actually became less common.
questions.rule: For an outcome claim, prefer the detail that measures the outcome itself rather than a possible reason for it.
questions.hint: The claim is about whether workers arrived late less often. Look for a before-and-after measure of late clock-ins, rather than a possible explanation from a survey or a recommendation about the pilot.

targets.text: During the eight weeks before the pilot, 11.8 percent of morning clock-ins were more than five minutes late.
During the staggered schedule, the rate was 6.4 percent.
A follow-up survey found that some employees on the 7:15 start said they could use a later public-bus connection instead of paying for a ride when they missed the earlier bus.
However, Park does not use the survey alone as proof of improved punctuality; the clock-in records are the direct measure of whether workers arrived on time.

sections.body: i1 ရဲ့ truck စောင့်ရတဲ့နှုန်း 38% ကနေ 17% ကျတာက Congestion လျော့တာကို ပြတယ်။ i2 ရဲ့ နောက်ကျတဲ့ clock-in 11.8% ကနေ 6.4% ကျတာက Punctuality ပိုကောင်းလာတာကို ပြတယ်။ i3 ရဲ့ labor hour တစ်နာရီအတွက် order 21.4 ကနေ 21.1 ဖြစ်တာက Productivity အနည်းငယ်ကျသွားပေမယ့် ယခင်အဆင့်နဲ့ နီးနေသေးတာကို ပြတယ်။ Evidence တစ်ခုကို တခြား claim အတွက် အလိုအလျောက် မသုံးသင့်ဘူး။

questions.prompt: Which detail most directly supports the claim that staggered starts improved employee punctuality?
questions.explanation: The clock-in comparison directly measures the outcome named in the claim: fewer workers arriving late.
questions.rule: A related explanation is not automatically the strongest evidence. Prefer the measure that directly answers the claim.

options.text: The entrance queue averaged fourteen vehicles during the pilot.
options.whyWrong: This supports the congestion claim, not punctuality.

options.text: Some workers said the later shift allowed them to catch a different bus.
options.whyWrong: This may help explain punctuality, but it does not directly measure whether late arrivals became less common.

options.text: Late morning clock-ins fell from 11.8 percent before the pilot to 6.4 percent during it.
Employees were allowed to request which start time they preferred.
options.whyWrong: This is a design limitation, not evidence that punctuality improved.

sections.body: ဒီမေးခွန်းမှာ punctuality တိုးတက်ခဲ့တယ်ဆိုတာကို သက်သေပြမယ့် detail လိုတယ်။ ဝန်ထမ်းတချို့ bus ပိုအဆင်ပြေတယ်လို့ ပြောတာက ဖြစ်ရတဲ့အကြောင်းကို ရှင်းပြနိုင်ပေမယ့် နောက်ကျတဲ့အရေအတွက် တကယ်လျော့သွားသလားဆိုတာကို မတိုင်းထားဘူး။

sections.title: A, B, C, D ကို စစ်ကြည့်မယ်
sections.body: C မှာ late clock-in 11.8% ကနေ 6.4% ထိ ကျသွားတာကို တိုက်ရိုက်နှိုင်းယှဉ်ထားလို့ မှန်တယ်။ A ရဲ့ entrance queue ၁၄ စီးက Congestion အကြောင်းပါ။ B ရဲ့ later bus က အကြောင်းရင်းတစ်ခုဖြစ်နိုင်ပေမယ့် punctuality result မဟုတ်ဘူး။ D ရဲ့ start time ရွေးခွင့်က pilot ရဲ့ ဒီဇိုင်းအချက်ဖြစ်ပြီး နောက်ကျမှုလျော့တာကို သက်သေမပြဘူး။

questions.prompt: Which evidence best supports Park's narrower claim that congestion improved without a large productivity loss?
questions.explanation: The claim contains two parts, so the best evidence must address both: substantially shorter truck waits and nearly unchanged output per labor hour.
questions.rule: For a two-part claim, check that the evidence covers both parts rather than proving only one.

options.text: Truck waits above fifteen minutes fell from 38 percent to 17 percent, while orders per labor hour changed only from 21.4 to 21.1.
Some employees could catch a later bus, and the road construction ended during the third week.
options.whyWrong: These details concern commuting and a possible traffic confound; they do not jointly measure congestion and productivity.

options.text: Late clock-ins fell to 6.4 percent, and damaged-order reports stayed nearly unchanged.
options.whyWrong: This pair addresses punctuality and one productivity-related measure, but not the congestion part of the claim.

options.text: The pilot lasted eight weeks, and workers could request their preferred start time.
options.whyWrong: These details describe the study design rather than evidence for the claimed operational results.

sections.title: Claim မှာ အချက်နှစ်ခုပါနေတယ်
sections.body: Park ရဲ့ claim က Congestion လျော့လာတယ်၊ ဒါပေမယ့် Productivity ကြီးကြီးမားမား မကျဘူးဆိုတဲ့ အပိုင်းနှစ်ခုပါ။ အဲဒါကြောင့် evidence တစ်ခုထဲမှာ truck စောင့်ချိန်အကြောင်းရော အလုပ်ပြီးမြောက်မှုနှုန်းအကြောင်းပါ ပါရမယ်။

sections.body: A မှာ ၁၅ မိနစ်ကျော် စောင့်ရတဲ့ truck 38% ကနေ 17% ကျတာနဲ့ labor hour တစ်နာရီအတွက် order 21.4 ကနေ 21.1 ပဲ ပြောင်းတာကို တွဲပြထားတယ်။ B က bus အသုံးပြုမှုနဲ့ လမ်းဆောက်လုပ်ရေးပြီးဆုံးမှုကို ပြောတာဖြစ်ပြီး claim နှစ်ပိုင်းလုံးကို မတိုင်းဘူး။ C က late clock-in နဲ့ damaged orders ကို ပြတယ်၊ Congestion မပါဘူး။ D က pilot ကြာချိန်နဲ့ start time ရွေးခွင့်ကို ဖော်ပြတာဖြစ်ပြီး ရလဒ်အတွက် evidence မဟုတ်ဘူး။

questions.prompt: Which pair contains one piece of evidence for each of Park's two reasons that the pilot deserves a longer trial: lower congestion and better punctuality?
questions.explanation: The queue count directly measures congestion and the clock-in rate directly measures punctuality, giving one clear evidence line for each reason.
questions.rule: When the question names two reasons, make sure the pair supplies direct evidence for both—not two facts about the same issue.

options.text: The entrance queue fell from twenty-six vehicles to fourteen; late clock-ins fell from 11.8 percent to 6.4 percent.
Orders per labor hour changed from 21.4 to 21.1; damaged-order reports stayed nearly unchanged.
options.whyWrong: Both details concern productivity or output quality, not one congestion measure plus one punctuality measure.

options.text: The road construction ended during the pilot; employees could request a preferred start time.
options.whyWrong: These are limitations or confounding factors, not evidence for the two benefits.

options.text: Some workers used a later bus; truck waiting above fifteen minutes fell to 17 percent.
options.whyWrong: The truck-wait figure directly supports congestion, but the bus comment is an explanation for some workers rather than the direct punctuality result.
